data.title: The China Auto Shock: Are Any Stocks Safe? — Barron's
data.description:
China has so much excess capacity to manufacture inexpensive, feature-laden electric vehicles and hybrids that it threatens car companies — and car stocks — everywhere.

By Al Root

China is upending the global auto industry.

The country has so much excess capacity to manufacture inexpensive, feature-laden electric vehicles and hybrids that it threatens car companies — and car stocks — everywhere.

The numbers are astounding, and growing: China is exporting 10 million vehicles this year, up from one million in 2020 — and it's just getting started. With roughly 100 auto makers operating at just 50% capacity, China sees foreign markets as a solution to years of chronic overbuilding.

The result is that auto workers from Wolfsburg, Germany, to Detroit may ultimately get caught in the maelstrom as car makers ditch models, and factories reduce production or close plants altogether.

Investors face hazards of their own. European car makers look uninvestible, at least for now. The Japanese, export giants of the past, face intense competition. U.S. car companies face similar hazards, but stocks of some, and some auto suppliers, do have appeal. Among the most promising: onetime giant General Motors and Lear, a global maker of seats and electrical systems. Even with the industry set on its ear, cars everywhere will still need parts.

European auto makers face the strongest floodwaters. China's share of European auto markets hit 10% in 2025, up from essentially zero in 2020. By 2030, that number could be closer to 17%. That's why some European car companies are trading for as little as three or four times year-ahead earnings, versus 14 for the Stoxx Europe 600 index. They're unlikely to improve anytime soon.

The outlook isn't much better for Japanese car makers. They sell far more cars abroad than in Japan, pitting them against China more often. They aren't winning. Chinese car makers recently started outselling Japanese brands in Europe.

The American market is in better shape because the domestic industry is protected for now from Chinese exports by tariffs and safety requirements. General Motors and Ford Motor also get most of their profits by selling big sport-utility vehicles and pickup trucks, whereas Chinese auto makers are focused on smaller vehicles.

With the still-healthy U.S. vehicle market the last best hope for non-Chinese car companies, everyone is focused on milking profits there. Volkswagen's Audi just announced its first U.S. plant in Georgia.

The Chinese aren't upending the world automotive industry with shoddy, low-end cars, but rather through excellence. Ford CEO Jim Farley's 2025 trips to China were "the most humbling thing I've ever seen....Their cost, their quality [are] far superior to what I see in the West."

Phone maker Xiaomi was once thought of as the Apple of China. But where Apple decided against moving into cars, Xiaomi put the pedal to the metal and started selling EVs in 2024. It sold some 430,000 over the past 12 months. That makes it bigger than Ford Motor in China and almost half the size of Tesla there.

Xiaomi's SU7 EV Max looks a lot like a Porsche Taycan, can go from zero to 60 miles an hour in a sizzling 2.5 seconds, and has a longer range and better tech features than the German luxury sports sedan. It costs $45,000. That compares with $100,000 and $240,000 for various Taycan models, meaning that buyers are paying at least an extra $55,000 for Porsche's prancing pony shield.

The SU7 has been devastating for Porsche. The German auto maker's Chinese sales dropped by a third in the first half of 2026, leading to a $7 billion write-off at Volkswagen, Porsche's main owner, and a restructuring plan at Porsche that contemplates cutting 25% of its workforce. Volkswagen is planning its own layoffs to compete.

For investors, meanwhile, Xiaomi's market win has been anything but. Its Hong Kong-traded shares have dropped 32% in 2026, while sales, operating profits, profit margins, and earnings estimates have all declined.

Xiaomi's problems are legion: Competition among the country's EV makers is intense, and government subsidies have disappeared while costs and global protectionism have risen.

That has left Xiaomi shares trading at 19 times earnings expected over the coming 12 months, while the company is expected to grow earnings at an average annual rate of almost 30% for the coming three years. That doesn't make Xiaomi stock a buy. Profit estimates are falling. Wall Street expects Xiaomi to generate about $4.8 billion in 2027 operating profit; a year ago, that estimate was $10.6 billion.

That's the story of the Chinese auto market in a nutshell. The industry has grown from an afterthought to an international behemoth. It's a sickly giant, though, lousy for investors, plagued by overcapacity, brutal competition, and weak profits, and in need of a restructuring that isn't coming.

China's impact is being felt everywhere. In 2025, Chinese cars captured 20% of the Australian market. Three in 10 new cars sold in Mexico originate from a Chinese-owned plant.

In Europe, a cap on imports imposed in October is looking like too little, too late. America could be next if its auto industry isn't careful.

"This is a knife fight. This is a wild environment," says AlixPartners global automotive market lead Mark Wakefield. "Chinese car makers grew up as Spartan warriors...born into violence from Day One."

China has become the world's largest new-passenger-vehicle market over the past two decades. Auto makers there sold roughly 30 million cars in 2025, as much as they sold in the U.S. and Europe combined. The Chinese cars are attractive, technologically advanced — and cheap. An all-electric BYD Song SUV with plenty of power, range, and advanced driving features costs roughly $25,000, almost 40% less than a comparable Tesla Model Y.

"The blow-your-mind-away moment is the number of cars that you see, and then you're like, 'Wait a second, that car costs this amount?' " says Barclays analyst Dan Levy.

China's journey to global dominance began decades ago, when it offered foreign auto makers market access in exchange for technology. Auto makers could sell into a huge potential market, but only through a joint venture with a local company. Tesla was allowed to own its own electric-vehicle capacity, but China benefited by gaining a technologically advanced EV supplier base.

"Tesla gave them the blueprint," adds Levy. Chinese auto makers make gasoline, hybrid, and all-electric cars. But the industry has leapfrogged Western companies by focusing on technologically advanced hybrid and electric cars.

Chinese auto makers develop new models in half the time it takes Western counterparts, and build their cars with low-cost labor at facilities supported by national and local government.

Chinese brands now account for roughly 70% of that nation's domestic sales, up from 35% a decade ago. Western brands have gone from selling roughly 15 million cars a year in China to 10 million while the overall market grew 50%.

An investor might think that market swing has benefited Chinese auto makers' stocks. It hasn't. The five largest Chinese auto makers are worth a combined $130 billion. That's roughly what Ford and General Motors are worth together, and a 12th of Tesla's market capitalization.

The problem is basic economics. China has massive overcapacity. It can make roughly twice as many cars as it sells. That is a disaster in high-fixed-cost manufacturing industries, says Wakefield. No surprise, then, that only a handful of Chinese auto makers turn a profit, and the ones that do, such as BYD, are less profitable than GM.

The solution to China's dilemma is obvious: Cut capacity. That isn't likely to happen. Capacity and jobs matter too much to local governments. That leaves China looking to export markets to fix its capacity problems. The 10 million vehicles it will export this year is a big number. The entire global light-vehicle market is roughly 80 million to 90 million units annually.

European regulators will protect the domestic industry with a mix of ever-strengthening quotas, tariffs, local sourcing requirements, joint ventures, and localization rules. That will give European auto stocks some relief. But Volkswagen and its peers are just starting their restructuring journeys, says Citi analyst Mike Ward, a process that America essentially completed during the 2008-09 financial crisis, culminating in the bankruptcy of both GM and Chrysler.

European auto makers fetch valuations that reflect these challenges. Volkswagen stock trades for 3.5 times earnings, Stellantis trades for four times earnings, and BMW trades for seven times. Even so, they probably aren't worth buying in the early days of a massive restructuring.

Chinese auto makers will arrive some day in the U.S. President Donald Trump said as much in January, announcing, "Let them come," at an event in Detroit.

To truly penetrate the U.S. market, Chinese auto makers must build American plants and distribution networks and staff them with American workers. That will take years.

For now, a bevy of barriers keeps the Chinese out. Tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles are essentially 100%. The Commerce Department's connected vehicle rule also bans Chinese software.

Another barrier is safety. European and Chinese rules assume that a passenger is wearing a seat belt when an air bag goes off. American rules don't. That means the air bag in an American vehicle needs to be bigger and more costly.

But relying on protectionist laws and big SUVs and pickups isn't a long-term strategic plan. Ford and GM need to keep lowering costs. Ford is trying to do that in Europe, forming a joint venture with Chinese auto maker Geely. The deal improves Ford's capacity utilization, while Geely gets local manufacturing.

American auto makers also need to build cheaper EVs. U.S. sales of all-electric cars plummeted after the $7,500 federal purchase tax credit expired in September 2025. But EV sales are expected to double by the end of the decade, and including hybrid, electrified vehicles could make up almost half of all new cars sold then.

Younger car buyers in the U.S. are also more apt to go electric. And the Chinese, when they come, will do so with an array of hybrid and electric vehicles that cost less and offer more features.

U.S. car makers know full well that they have to improve before that happens. Ford's Universal Electric Vehicle platform is designed to produce an all-electric midsize truck for $30,000 that will hit the market in 2027. GM's fourth-generation EVs will use new battery chemistries and fewer drive-unit parts to lower costs in 2028. It recently announced plans to build hybrid electric vehicles in Lansing, Mich.

GM also plans to cut new-car development time in half, partly by using artificial intelligence. "The faster we can iterate, the better your car will get," says GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson.

Lower-priced cars represent the ultimate protection from China. The average price for a new car in the U.S. is $50,562, according to automotive data provider Kelley Blue Book, up about $13,000 from prepandemic levels. The average EV price is $55,879. If new-car buyers are to consider a domestic electric, there must be more affordable options.

Ford and GM remain investible today in a way their European and Chinese counterparts just aren't. Of the two, GM looks like the better bet right now because of how it allocates capital.

Since Paul Jacobson became chief financial officer in late 2020, GM has repurchased some $30 billion in stock. Shares outstanding have fallen from 1.4 billion to less than 850 million — and more buybacks are coming. The auto maker is doing it without adding any debt. GM has consistently generated $10 billion or more in annual free cash flow in recent years.

Buying back stock makes perfect sense, given GM's combination of low valuation and strong free cash flow. It's expected to generate cash flow of $11 billion in 2027. That would purchase about 130 million shares at current levels. Retiring that stock would drive 18% earnings-per-share growth in 2027 even if net income was flat.

GM also reports roughly $87 billion in plants and equipment on its books. The entire company, adjusting for debt and the financing company, is valued at about $55 billion. It's as if GM is buying its car capacity — forgetting all of its other assets — for 60 cents on the dollar. Anyone building a new-car plant in the U.S. won't get that discount.

Ford isn't likely to pursue a similar buyback path. Dual-class voting shares and Ford family ownership mean that the company prefers dividends to buying back shares. Currently, the stock yields 5.1%.

Parts companies, in theory, should be agnostic to who sells the cars as long as they supply everyone.

Investors still need to be careful. Take Aptiv, which supplies safety and electronics systems. Its parts are in more than half of the top 20 cars in China. That didn't stop a 17% drop after the company reported second-quarter earnings. A weakening Chinese market affected production schedules for all car companies, and Europeans are exporting fewer vehicles to China.

Power and data-connection company TE Connectivity avoided an Aptiv-like outcome, growing its calendar-year third-quarter car business 6%. TE, which makes high-voltage cables for EVs, serves other industries including data centers, which is a tailwind for growth, according to Baird analyst Luke Junk. He rates shares Outperform and has a $250 price target, up 12% from recent levels.

A favorite parts stock of Citi's Ward is Lear. He rates shares Buy and has a $179 price target, up more than 50% from recent levels. "They stick to their knitting," says Ward. "They make seats and generate cash."

Like GM, Lear consistently buys its own stock. Shares outstanding dropped from 58.7 million to 49.3 million over the past three years. Free cash flow in 2027 is expected to be $600 million, about 10% of Lear's market value. The S&P 500 index free-cash-flow yield is closer to 4%.

Picking car stock winners won't be easy. The storm is just beginning. American, European, and Japanese car makers need to up their game to escape the floodwaters.

Write to Al Root at allen.root@dowjones.com

data.title: Tech Trader: Anthropic Partners Face Enormous Counterparty Risk — Barron's
THE BIG MONEY POLL — Barron's
data.description:
The optimists in Barron's fall poll cite robust earnings growth; the pessimists see a bubble in danger of bursting. Plus, the pros' forecasts for rates, midterms, and more.

By Paul R. La Monica

There is plenty to worry about in the current investment climate, if you're so inclined. Bond yields soared this past summer, interest rates look set to rise, and the artificial-intelligence boom that has powered the economy and stock market for the past few years may be unsustainable. But there is just as much — if not more — to celebrate, including a healthy economy, robust growth in corporate earnings, and the likelihood that the same AI boom will continue for several more years, at least.

Half the money managers responding to Barron's fall Big Money poll take the sunny view, calling themselves bullish about the outlook for U.S. stocks over the next 12 months. Based on their mean response, the bulls forecast that the Dow Jones Industrials will rise another 9% by the end of 2027.

The Big Money bulls are optimistic about the trajectory of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, too, predicting that the two equity indexes will gain 8% and 13%, respectively, by the end of next year. They see the S&P 500 ending 2027 at 8366, and the Nasdaq finishing next year at 29,527.

"The AI capex [capital expenditure] cycle will continue in 2027," says Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management in Boston. "People underestimate that. Spending in the late-1990s [dot-com era] bubble days lasted for eight years. It has been just four years since the launch of ChatGPT. Investors need to gravitate to where the earnings growth is, profit margins are, and opportunity exists."

Harris Nydick, co-managing member of CFS Investment Advisory Services in Totowa, N.J., agrees. The stock market is "still in the early innings" of the AI boom, he says, adding that the S&P 500 could climb as high as 9000 before this market cycle turns.

The bulls' ranks have thinned slightly this fall from 54% in our spring survey. The bears' camp has grown, measuring 24% of respondents, up from 17% in April. Some 26% of managers now call themselves neutral on the market outlook, slightly lower than in the spring.

Forty percent of managers consider the market overvalued, while 10% say stocks are undervalued, roughly on par with the spring poll.

Bill Smead, chief investment officer at Smead Capital Management in Phoenix, is a Big Money bear who thinks stocks are overpriced. Too much of the U.S. market is leveraged to the AI trade, he says. "All of this capital is crammed into one sector. That's a risk to the economy and the markets," says Smead.

Amy Robinson, CEO of Robinson Value Management in San Antonio, calls herself neutral on stocks but similarly sees risks in AI-related companies' strategies and their shares. Robinson calls Nvidia the market's most overvalued stock, saying its investments in customers remind her of the circular vendor financing of the dot-com era. Nvidia has helped fund or guarantee loans for many customers' purchases of Nvidia chips, which are central to AI compute.

Barron's conducts the Big Money poll, a survey of professional investors, twice yearly, with the help of Erdos Media Research in Ramsey, N.J. The latest poll, completed Sept. 23 to Oct. 15, drew responses from 81 investment professionals from around the country.

The survey period was a choppy one for stocks, as bond yields rose sharply in late September and then retreated. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point at its Sept. 15-16 meeting, just ahead of the survey's launch.

The higher cost of capital and the strength and longevity of "the AI trade" are top of mind for many Big Money pros. Twenty-seven percent of respondents call a potential AI slowdown the biggest risk the market will face in the next six months. The same percentage say rising interest rates are the biggest worry, while 17% cite higher bond yields.

The Fed's policy committee voted to leave the federal-funds rate target range unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% at its Oct. 28-29 meeting. But with inflation still well above the Fed's 2% annual target, futures traders place roughly 75% odds on another quarter-point rate increase in December.

"I appreciate that rates have been this high before, but there has been a huge and rapid repricing in the fixed-income market," says Joe Gilbert, a portfolio manager at Integrity Asset Management in Rocky River, Ohio.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield hit a 24-year high of 5.36% in early October, up from 4.80% at the start of September — a huge move in yield terms. It has since retreated to just below 5%.

The outlook for tech stocks, in particular AI-related names, is polarizing for the Big Money crowd, as it is for the market generally. The S&P 500 has made almost no headway since mid-August amid growing concerns about the cost of the AI buildout and the ultimate payoff from this revolutionary technology.

Thirty-one percent of Big Money managers consider information technology the most attractive sector for the next 12 months, followed by healthcare, at 26%. Yet 22% of poll respondents think info tech is the least attractive sector.

Lori Keith, a portfolio manager at San Francisco-based Parnassus Investments, is a tech bull. "There are high expectations and tech is a crowded trade, but these are still early days around adoption for AI," she says.

Just 37% of poll respondents think current corporate spending on AI infrastructure will yield a positive return in the next 24 months. Thirty-two percent think it won't, and the remainder say it is too soon to know.

David Hartzell, president and CEO of Cornell Capital Management in Clarence Center, N.Y., says AI will be "mind-boggling for the next decade." The challenge, he says, is picking long-term winners, or "the individual stocks that will be around in the next 10 years."

Hartzell is sticking with an index fund, the Vanguard S&P 500 exchange-traded fund, which trades under the ticker VOO. "If you buy VOO, you get all the good stocks, and the bad stocks will eventually drop out of the picture," he says. "It's the best way to play the tech boom."

Much of the bullish case for U.S. stocks rests on the outlook for corporate earnings, which has seldom, if ever, been so rosy — again, largely due to tech-related spending. S&P 500 earnings per share are on track to grow 34.4% this year to $362.89, according to estimates gathered by FactSet, and about 16% in 2027 to $420.43.

Most Big Money respondents are also counting on decent earnings growth next year, although they aren't as ebullient as industry analysts. Forty percent of poll participants forecast that corporate earnings will grow at least 11% in 2027, with about a third predicting profits will rise a more modest 6% to 10%, roughly in line with the historic average.

"You can have sector corrections, but the market as a whole still looks attractive because earnings are going up," says Kayvan Karoon, president and CEO of KS Capital Management in Rochelle Park, N.J.

The S&P 500 currently trades for 18.4 times 2027 estimates, slightly below the five-year average of 19.3 and down from 22.7 in January. "Unless you think earnings are going to collapse, this isn't an expensive valuation," says Jose Medeiros, managing partner at Stonerise Capital Partners in San Francisco. "People expect a deceleration in earnings growth, and there are still lofty expectations. But they probably will be met."

Hal Andersen, co-founder and partner at Soltis Investment Advisors in St. George, Utah, says he is "amazed by the strength in profitability." He expects the tech sector to continue leading on earnings growth, while other sectors contribute more gains in coming months.

Nearly half of the Big Money managers expect U.S. stocks to outperform other markets in the next 12 months. Yet 71% say they are bullish on non-U.S. equities, and 38% plan to increase their allocation to non-U.S. stocks over the next year. European banks are especially attractive, says Ryan Payne, president of Payne Capital Management in New York. "I see more profit growth ahead for them, and there are more catalysts to move them," he says, noting that lending growth should strengthen as the European Union economy improves.

About a quarter of poll respondents think emerging markets will perform best in the year ahead. But Louis Lau, director of investments at San Diego's Brandes Investment Partners and co-manager of the Brandes Emerging Markets Value fund, cautions against great expectations. "One big concern is that in times of higher U.S. yields and interest rates and higher oil prices, you also have a higher dollar," he says. "That isn't the best setup for EM."

Bonds still don't have many fans among the Big Money crowd, which has largely been bearish on fixed income for several years. (Bond prices move inversely to yields.) But the disdain isn't universal. "After years of suffering, you can now grab yield," says Cesar Manent, principal at 5th Street Advisors in Stamford, Conn. "One of our biggest themes is to own a lot of income-generating assets. You can do that on the bond side with short duration of around three years."

With the Fed expected to raise interest rates again in coming months, many bond investors favor shorter-duration investments. They are less sensitive to rate changes than longer-duration assets and allow for quicker reinvestment when rates rise.

Two-thirds of poll respondents think the federal-funds rate will end this year in a range of 4% to 4.25%, implying one rate increase at the Fed's December policy meeting. Forty-three percent think the fed-funds rate will be higher than 4.25% by the end of next year. Just 10% think rates are too restrictive at current levels, while 54% think rates are just right.

Kevin Warsh, who became Fed chairman in May, gets a round of applause from the Big Money men and women for his conduct of monetary policy; 71% view him favorably. Andersen, of Soltis, thinks Warsh is in a tough spot, and he isn't alone. "Inflation is hot, the energy component in particular," says Andersen. "We're still hopeful that the [Iran] war can end and oil markets will return to normal. The Fed may not have to keep raising rates then."

Fiscal policy is another matter. Only 5% of managers give the Trump administration an A for its conduct of fiscal policy, while 60% grade the White House D or F. Lau doled out a failing grade, blaming it on "the combination of tariffs and lack of a coherent plan to bring more manufacturing back to the U.S."

Sandra S. Martin, managing director of Martin Investment Management, which has offices in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., and Evanston, Ill., is more blunt. "There is no constructive fiscal policy," she says, calling the president's tariff policy "like shooting yourself in the foot."

Tim Ewing, managing director of Mesirow Financial Investment Management in Chicago, says the fiscal backdrop concerns him. "You have a government that is spending out of control, so it can't be surprising to see that the 10-year Treasury yield is up," he says.

The managers see a change coming in government, if not in policy. Eighty-four percent expect the Democrats to win control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, although two-thirds think the Republicans will retain control of the Senate.

Our fall poll finds only 51% of respondents beating the S&P 500's performance this year both personally and professionally. That speaks to the investment challenges posed by the market's concentration in tech and a changing macro backdrop. It also may explain the divergence of sentiment in our latest Big Money poll.

Write to Paul R. La Monica at paul.lamonica@barrons.com

data.title: Proposition 40 Is a Big Tech Referendum — Barron's
data.description:
Fight or Flight. "I left my heart in San Francisco," the late Tony Bennett sang back in 1962, in his ballad about decamping from the Bay Area for pastures new. Bennett may soon win some new fans among California's uber-wealthy tech elite.

By Nate Wolf

The reason is Proposition 40, a state ballot measure that would impose a one-time wealth tax on California's 250-odd billionaires primarily to backfill healthcare cuts by the Trump administration. Opponents argue that could prompt tech moguls and their venture capital backers to leave San Francisco — if they haven't already — taking their fortunes, tax dollars, and business interests with them.

The response from some Californians is "good riddance."

In a September poll by the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies, 45% of likely voters in California supported Prop 40, while 42% opposed it.

In recent years, Big Tech has cozied up with the Trump administration and dodged child-safety and antitrust scrutiny without many meaningful consequences beyond the occasional fine or slap on the wrist. All the while, tech stocks and start-up valuations have ballooned. Tech companies now account for almost 40% of the S&P 500.

That dynamic hasn't won the industry many fans: As their wealth and influence grow, distrust in large tech companies has hit a record high. In Gallup polling in 2026, 41% of U.S. adults said they have little or no trust in the sector.

"The ardent love affair between America, and particularly blue-state America, with tech has ended," says Margaret O'Mara, a historian of the industry at the University of Washington. Where the tech sector was long seen as a bastion of liberalism, progress, and utopian promises, many now see its billionaire leaders as 21st-century robber barons.

A breakup could get particularly messy in the Golden State, where the tech sector accounts for 73% of Californian billionaires' wealth. That is according to three University of California, Berkeley economists, two of whom, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, helped design Prop 40. They don't count the venture capital financiers on Sand Hill Road or some crypto and fintech CEOs at firms like Coinbase Global and Robinhood Markets.

The Prop 40 vote will be an indicator of whether tech's public-relations problem has consequences. Should the measure fail, history shows the tech industry may feel emboldened to expand its political influence further. If the proposition succeeds, expect industry leaders to question whether California is their long-term home while states like Florida and Texas wait in the wings as low-tax tech-and-crypto hubs.

"We are sending a national signal," warns Robert Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable. "That California is no longer a place where you want to come and be an innovator."

Deep-Pocketed Resistance

If Prop 40 wasn't about tech to begin with, it sure is now, after hundreds of millions of dollars have flowed into the campaign from Silicon Valley.

SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, California's healthcare union, conceived of Prop 40 last year to address the loss of Medicaid funding from President Donald Trump's sweeping 2025 tax and spending bill. The cuts could cause 1.3 million Californians to lose healthcare over the next four years, says the nonpartisan California Budget & Policy Center.

If Prop 40 passes, a billionaire residing in California as of Jan. 1, 2026, will pay a one-time tax of 5% of their fortune either upfront or in yearly installments. Saez and Zucman estimate the measure could raise about $100 billion. If all goes well, Saez would like to see a permanent annual billionaire tax at a more modest rate. He floated 1% in an interview with Barron's.

While business groups, several other unions, and even Gov. Gavin Newsom have coalesced against Prop 40, tech luminaries are doing the heavy lifting.

At the start of the year, Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former CEO Eric Schmidt helped found Building a Better California, a political action committee that has contributed $135 million to defeat the proposition, per campaign finance disclosures. The PAC has also spent roughly $212 million to fund two separate initiatives, Propositions 41 and 42, which would nullify Prop 40 if they win by a bigger margin.

The heavy spending may be worth it for Schmidt and Brin — combined net worth some $300 billion, per Forbes data — but it is also evidence of the exact financial and political might that many voters fear. But such campaigns have backfired in the past: In 2019, Seattle voters rejected a slate of City Council candidates backed by Amazon.com, which poured $1.5 million into the local race.

"Here in the Bay Area, we've been flooded with 'vote no' ads on the Big Tech platforms we maintain as our bosses and other billionaires put over a hundred million dollars into defeating the measure," says one Alphabet employee, speaking on condition of anonymity. "The fact that they can do this is also quite concerning."

Rank-and-file tech workers face a unique choice in the election. Nearly 100,000 Californians work for Nvidia, Meta Platforms, Google, and Salesforce alone, according to estimates from Revelio Labs. That is just a few of the tech companies run by the state's billionaires. In other words, a significant cohort of voters in bright-blue San Francisco will directly decide whether to tax their bosses, many of whom have been outspoken critics of Prop 40.

Politics aside, who hasn't had a boss they would have loved to see taken down a peg?

Economic Exodus or Idle Threats?

The implicit threat from Prop 40's billionaire opponents is that they will leave California altogether if the initiative passes. You know how the saying goes: If you bite the hand that feeds, the hand will buy a lakefront compound in Nevada — or something like that.

Mark Zuckerberg, the CEO of Meta, made that ultimatum explicit. Zuck told a special committee of Meta's board in August that he would establish residency outside the state before the Nov. 3 election, according to a recent regulatory filing. Within a week, the board moved to create a new class of shares that will allow Zuckerberg to pay the tax without diluting his voting rights.

"We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure," said Susan Li, Meta's Chief Financial Officer. "It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we're seeing across every part of our business driven by AI."

Joshua Rauh, an economist at Stanford, and Benjamin Jaros, a researcher at the right-leaning Hoover Institution, most recently estimated Prop 40 would collect only $28 billion to $36 billion and permanently shrink the state's income tax revenue. The main reason for the disagreement is that no one knows who left the state before Jan. 1 or who will leave in the years to come.

To be sure, cities across America are salivating at the opportunity to pull start-ups and tech workers away from Silicon Valley, says Libby Schaaf, CEO of the Bay Area Council and the former Democratic mayor of Oakland.

"I can tell you, every big city mayor is looking to steal our talent," Schaaf says. "Every big city mayor is looking to steal our economic engine of innovation." Prop 40, she adds, would put California at a long-term disadvantage to other states.

California is faring just fine for now. Companies based in the state have attracted a record-shattering $371 billion in venture capital in 2026, per PitchBook, thanks in large part to the AI boom. The other 49 states have drawn $145 billion combined.

The real downside for the tech industry may be more subtle. Silicon Valley has thrived in part because successful entrepreneurs put their money and energy back into the tech ecosystem, says Nate, a tech founder who requested we omit his surname because of his role at a large software company. California has long had high taxes and pricey real estate, sure, but the state valued innovators who stuck around to help young founders. Prop 40 could disrupt that cycle, Nate argues.

"There's a little bit of, I wouldn't say souring on the Bay Area, but just kind of a feeling like they're not welcome," he says of the wealthiest friends in his network.

If the money pouring into Prop 40 opposition is any indication, the most powerful tech leaders won't pack their bags without a fight. In fact, the potential afterglow of victory on Election Day will embolden the industry to push for even more influence, predicts Dan Schnur, a veteran California political strategist.

Schnur sees echoes of TechNet, a lobbying group he assisted in the 1990s, which formed in opposition to a 1996 California ballot initiative to make shareholder lawsuits easier. Three decades after thwarting that ballot measure, the organization now has a legal center, a headquarters in Washington, and a PAC that has made political donations every cycle since 1998.

"Winning is always very motivational," Schnur explains. "In all likelihood, [Prop 40] is going to encourage this generation of tech leaders to become more politically involved going forward."

The bad news for the billionaires is that the proponents of Prop 40 won't quit either. If anything, Prop 40 has exposed a rupture in California that will widen in the years to come.

"If Prop 40 is defeated, its opponents should not take false comfort," Schnur says. "There are more billionaires in the world today than ever before. And billionaires are less popular than ever before."

Tech executives will have to reckon with that conundrum — whether they leave California or not.

data.title: Income Investing: Tax-Loss Harvesting in Bonds? It's a Big Deal. — Barron's
data.description:
By Amey Stone

Tax-loss harvesting — selling a security that fell in price in order to use the loss to offset gains elsewhere in a portfolio — was a significant opportunity for bond investors in the third quarter.

That is thanks to a rapid rise in yields, as bond prices move inversely to interest rates. Many investors took advantage of that opportunity, particularly in municipal bonds.

In fact, so many investors sold their munis that it may have exacerbated already painful losses. Munis fell 6.4% in the third quarter compared with about a 3% decline for corporate bonds and Treasuries. Bond prices have since rebounded, so tax-loss opportunities are now less available. Still, the deluge of tax-related selling sheds light on how two important investing trends — the popularity of tax-advantaged automatic investing programs and the growth of exchange-traded funds — are reshaping market dynamics.

Tax-loss harvesting activity in municipal bonds is a familiar headwind whenever municipal bonds have a rough year, "but this year was unprecedented," says Jeff Timlin, lead portfolio manager for municipal bond strategies at Sage Advisory. "I've never seen anything like it." Trading volume in munis in September nearly doubled from the average of the first seven months of 2026, says Brian Barney, a portfolio manager on the fixed-income team at Parametric.

"It was kind of off the charts," says Duane McAllister, a senior portfolio manager and co-leader of the municipal sector at Baird. "We've had more trading related to tax-loss harvesting than we've ever seen, and the interesting thing is that tax losses weren't nearly as large as they have been at other points in time," he says, referencing selloffs during the pandemic in 2020 and in April 2025, after President Donald Trump announced tariffs on so-called Liberation Day.

Why the increase?

For starters, there are a lot of investors looking to diversify out of highly appreciated stocks who could use those losses to offset the gains. Plus, the growth in automated tax-loss harvesting offered by many asset managers is a likely factor. Parametric's offering, available to accounts over $125,000, automatically looks for tax-loss harvesting opportunities when a bond has declined more than 3%, says Barney.

Another trend at work: Investors are moving from mutual funds to more tax-efficient exchange-traded funds. Tax-loss harvesting may have created the impetus for some investors to make the switch, since exchanging an active mutual fund for an index ETF generally avoids the wash-sale rule. (You can't take a tax deduction for a loss on the sale of a security if you purchased another security that is essentially the same 30 days before or after the sale.)

Since the beginning of September, open-end mutual funds experienced net outflows of nearly $30 billion, while muni ETFs picked up $20 billion in inflows, Barney says.

Tax-loss harvesting happened in other areas of the bond market, but it didn't have the same impact as on the muni market, says Barney. That's because the corporate bond market is larger and more liquid. Also, taxable bonds are often held in tax-deferred accounts, where tax-loss selling doesn't make sense.

While the tax-loss harvesting opportunity is largely over, the impact of all that activity remains, says Sage's Timlin. Munis' after-tax yields "were as attractive as they had been in 20-plus years," he says, but investors looking to buy individual bonds when trading activity was at a peak found it challenging.

While there are minimal transaction costs for trading in ETFs these days, fund managers argue there are other hidden costs for muni investors. For example, the data suggest that investors bought index funds as a placeholder, planning to get back into an actively managed fund when the wash-sale rule was no longer a factor. Now they are effectively stuck in them since selling would trigger a short-term gain, which could erase the benefit of harvesting the tax loss, says Timlin.

Plus, they may not be in an optimal position in terms of security selection or the overall interest-rate sensitivity of their muni portfolio. The iShares National Muni Bond ETF is underperforming about 60% of municipal bond funds year to date, according to Morningstar.

McAllister calls that "leakage." He says: "If you stay in the new investment, it may not be exactly what you wanted. There is a cost, but it is hard to quantify."

data.title: Funds: How the New Crypto ETFs Value Their Assets — Barron's
data.description:
By Lewis Braham

What is Microsoft worth? Most active fund managers would be able to make an estimate based on its historical cash flows.

Now try that with cryptocurrencies. Bitcoin produces no cash flow, so it's difficult to evaluate. Yet there are now some 75 actively managed crypto exchange-traded funds, according to Morningstar. Most don't employ traditional fundamental analysis, but one in particular — the newly launched T. Rowe Price Active Crypto — does, depending on the currency.

Manager Blue Macellari sees Bitcoin as a "macro asset" like gold, and analyzes its supply-and-demand dynamics and the economy's inflationary outlook. She studies other cryptos for the value of their blockchain technology. Some, such as Solana and Avalanche, can produce cash flow by what is called "staking," where investors effectively lease their coins to maintain the blockchain network's integrity, receiving a share of currencies' transaction fees. Solana and Avalanche are "supereasy" to perform a modified discounted cash-flow model on, she says.

Yet Macellari acknowledges that crypto price trends — as opposed to underlying fundamentals — still play a major role. "One of the things that makes fundamental analysis in crypto both so interesting and at times unbelievably frustrating is that all the blockchains are like living, breathing things, and they don't stick to an earnings schedule," she says. "You have all the data all the time." The prices of cryptocurrencies can move more swiftly and violently than any gradual shift in fundamental outlooks.

Since its July inception, T. Rowe's tiny $24 million ETF is up some 24%, about on par with the behemoth $65 billion iShares Bitcoin Trust. Other active ETFs have had more time to prove themselves. Many employ options strategies to generate income from crypto's volatility, as the more volatile an asset is, the higher the premium it pays to options sellers.

The $248 million Nicholas Crypto Income ETF has a distribution rate of 36% from selling, or "writing," put options on Bitcoin and Ether — about half its portfolio — and crypto-related stocks such as the volatile BitMine Immersion Technologies. Puts, which give holders the right to sell an asset at a set price within a specific period, generate income without capping any crypto upside. However, this strategy can actually accentuate losses in a downturn if done incorrectly.

Manager David Nicholas can also buy put options to hedge if crypto markets turn ugly. He uses technical indicators based on price trends, not fundamental analysis, to decide when to hedge. Currently, the ETF is unhedged, he says, but it has been hedged often during a difficult 2026. As a result, since the ETF's inception in June 2025, it has notched a cumulative 10.7% loss when including its hefty options payouts, versus iShares Bitcoin's 26.7% loss, according to Morningstar.

Another Bitcoin options ETF, Fortuna Hedged Bitcoin, hedges routinely, selling call options to generate income to pay for defensive put options. "It's Bitcoin exposure with guardrails," says manager Mark Adams, adding that his ETF is more for the "crypto curious" than die-hards. Since its March 2025 inception, the ETF has significantly outperformed Bitcoin during downturns but lagged behind after big rallies. (Calls give holders the right to buy an asset at a set price within a specific period.)

The Arrow Valtoro ETF employs systematic quantitative models that include price trends and other macroeconomic factors to determine whether to be in cash, Bitcoin, or gold bullion. Since its October 2025 inception, it's down 2%, while the iShares Bitcoin ETF is down 26%.

The largest active ETF, the $1.4 billion NEOS Bitcoin High Income, has a simpler covered-call options strategy to generate income. Call options limit the upside for their sellers, but NEOS doesn't write options on the whole portfolio to generate its 25% to 30% target distribution. It can sometimes get that payout with options written on half the portfolio.

Since its October 2024 inception, NEOS is up 13% cumulatively, including options payouts, versus the iShares Bitcoin ETF's 17%. In the past 12 months, it's down 27% versus the iShares ETF's 28% loss.

data.title: Equinox Gold Is a Diamond in the Rough — Barron's
data.description:
The company has quietly transformed its operations. Shares are a buy.

By Jacob Sonenshine

Out of all the ways to benefit from a potential gold rally, buying stock in the $12 billion miner Equinox Gold is among the best.

This might seem an arbitrary take, given the many publicly traded gold miners. But Vancouver-based Equinox, which is covered by just 13 Wall Street analysts, is more a diamond in the rough than a mere beneficiary of higher gold prices. With multiple published materials every quarter (its second-quarter summary runs 43 pages), it's a fairly communicative company that's on the doorstep of demonstrating productivity improvements in several of its six mines. It could therefore boost its valuation toward the rest of the industry, and of course would see its earnings explode higher if gold prices do the same.

This scenario would likely spark larger stock gains for Equinox than for other miners, thanks to its lower valuation. The industry would see profit expectations rise, while Equinox's self-help story would give it the kicker of an expanding price/earnings multiple.

This thesis begins with the argument for higher gold prices. The precious metal is down 24% from its record high in January, to about $4,050 an ounce. That isn't surprising, given that it has about doubled in the past three years, almost begging traders to take profits. But like clockwork, it always sees support above the roughly $3,900-to-$4,000 area, where buyers have swooped in all year to stabilize the price. Even with the recent dip, gold remains in its larger uptrend of the past three years, suggesting buying support is close by.

"We look at this as another generational opportunity to get into gold at a relatively low basis," says Ben McMillan, chief investment officer at IDX Advisors. "The upside for gold is extremely robust."

Sparking some of that upside would likely be central banks, which are diversifying their reserves away from U.S. dollars in the face of geopolitical tensions. The third-largest buyer in the second quarter, central banks and other institutions increased their net purchases of ounces by over 400% quarter over quarter, according to the World Gold Council. They tend to buy more on dips, which should give gold-related investors confidence in the commodity's long-term trajectory.

"Central banks are not speculators," McMillan says. "If ever there was a buy-the-dip participant, it's those guys when it comes to gold."

Higher gold prices mean earnings gains for miners — including Equinox, which saw almost all of its $770 million in second-quarter revenue from gold. When the price of gold rises, expected sales rise. Miners have many fixed costs, such as depreciation and other exploration costs that don't change quickly. So, higher sales means higher profit margins, sending earnings up by a larger percentage than sales.

Just imagine what would happen to earnings estimates if gold reclaims its record high, 31% above current levels. Equinox would participate in the party, with the added tailwind of operational improvements.

It just acquired Orla Mining, which has two mines, one in Mexico and the other in Canada. The deal, a mostly stock transaction that closed in July, increases Equinox's overall operating profit margin as the two Orla mines carry higher profit margins after accounting for all-in sustaining costs per mine versus Equinox's mines. The company's 2026 guidance implies it expects Orla's mines to produce almost 400,000 ounces of gold annually, about one-third of the company's expected 1.1 million ounces.

If the market sees that Equinox is integrating Orla without surprise costs or hiccups, it will price the higher margins into the stock. Often, the market remains skeptical of an acquirer until it sees successful integration, a risk to the story, but there's currently no reason to doubt it.

"The integration will wrap up by the end of this year," Jason Simpson, incoming Equinox CEO and former Orla CEO, tells Barron's. "We're well on our way to that."

Two other Equinox mines, Greenstone and Valentine, both in Canada, have room for improved margins. Their profits per ounce of production lags behind those for "senior" gold producers — slightly larger miners Equinox aspires to rival, namely Kinross Gold, Alamos Gold, and Agnico Eagle Mines.

That's where Equinox's "trommel" comes in. That's a machine that sorts out certain earth material during the mining process to pull out more gold-bearing rock faster. The company is installing the trommel this year. Current and outgoing CEO Darren Hall said on the second-quarter earnings call that the company will see some benefits of the equipment before year end.

Any update from the company in the third or fourth quarter that the trommel is unlocking more gold production at Greenstone would catalyze stock gains, as the market would anticipate higher margins there. More production in mining or excavating businesses typically translates into more market share for the producer. Revenue per mine would rise much faster than cost per mine, given that most of the mine's fixed costs are already in place. Sure, a glitch with the trommel is a risk, but it might not crush the stock from here, given that the relatively small valuation already reflects subpar operations for Equinox.

"We expect valuation multiples will expand as the flagship Greenstone and Valentine mines ramp up production," writes BMO analyst Kevin O'Halloran, who has a $15.70 price target on the U.S.-traded shares, which equates to a 50% gain from Wednesday's close of $10.48.

For areas near Valentine, the company announced early this year it's using "Dora AI," an artificial-intelligence-powered software program that identifies promising exploration areas. Here, as well, Equinox is making a small investment to enhance gold production. Overall, Greenstone's and Valentine's productivity should improve over the coming quarters.

Greater productivity and margins would create a larger and more stable miner in Equinox — lifting the valuation. Currently trading at about 7.6 times forward earnings, the stock would rerate closer to the near 12 times for the VanEck Gold Miners exchange-traded fund. Just returning to par with the industry — where Equinox traded before the Orla merger — would increase the stock by 51%. That's even before considering higher earnings from rising gold prices.

The main risk is that the price of gold could fall below recent support. Sure, a slow Orla integration or scant updates on the trommel are the main company-specific risks, but another leg higher in interest rates would push gold to the next level of support, at about $3,700, because a higher risk-free rate of return would compete against gold's appeal. But that's far from a certain outcome, given that rates have stabilized for weeks now, after having priced in a lot of inflation.

In Equinox, investors can strike gold.

data.title: Energy Giants Are Awash in Cash. Will They Spend It? — Barron's
Consider Annuities to Avoid Bond Drama — Barron's
Brazil's Market Rout Creates More Bargains — Barron's
data.description:
By Craig Mellow

A fourth term for the left-leaning Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is bad news from markets' point of view. But is it bad enough to justify a 7% plunge in the real and two percentage point leap in yields on 10-year government bonds following Lula's surprise Oct. 25 victory?

No, thinks Graham Stock, senior sovereign strategist at RBC BlueBay Asset Management. "There's been an overshoot relative to deterioration in the fundamentals," he says.

Most of Stock's competitors agree in the short term. "We are looking for a bottom and patiently scaling in," says Christopher Hays, an emerging markets debt portfolio manager at TCW.

Longer-term prospects depend on reading the 81-year-old Lula's mind, among other known unknowns.

Volatile Brazilian equities are a niche play for the strong-of-stomach. The near-$1 trillion bond market attracts investors far and wide for the highest "real yields" (return minus inflation) of any decently liquid market. Those same yields are threatening a crisis for Brazil's perennially overspending government and increasingly indebted population alike.

The sovereign 10-year yield is around 15% annually, with inflation less than 5%. Bank loans average more than 60%. Credit cards frequently charge triple digits. "No country can function with real rates of 10%," says Arthur Budaghyan, chief emerging markets strategist at BCA Research.

Hawkish paranoia is embedded in Brazil's central bankers after a decade of runaway inflation in the 1980s and '90s. Monetary loosening will depend on Lula shrinking a budget deficit, approaching 10% of gross domestic product, says Steven Schoenfeld, CEO of MarketVector Indexes. "The only way to lower interest rates is to see some positive signs on fiscal policy," he says.

Lula generated few such signs in the third term he is just completing. More than 90% of Brazilian state spending is set automatically through a web of indexation schemes, making cuts doubly challenging for any government.

The good news is that Brazil is flush with cash, points out Thierry Larose, portfolio manager for emerging markets local debt at Vontobel Asset Management. The central bank is sitting on more than $360 billion in currency reserves as commodity exports boom. Foreigners hold just 10% or so of local-currency bonds, minimizing the risk of a "hot money" run. "Brazil is not facing a liquidity crisis, still less a solvency crisis," Larose says.

Fourth-term Lula hardly needs shock therapy to stem the vicious cycle of mounting debt pushing mountainous interest rates, TCW's Hays says. A primary budget surplus (not counting interest payments) of 1% of GDP would "be taken positively by markets," he predicts.

Budaghyan's BCA sees a less investor-friendly escape from the rate straitjacket: the central bank printing money to buy government debt, known in the developed world as quantitative easing. For Brazil's more fragile economy, this policy will result in "massive" currency devaluation, unleashing inflation and crushing bondholders. "Basically, Brazil needs to do QE," he says. "But then where does the currency go?"

Which path to expect depends considerably on armchair psychoanalysis of Lula, who was first elected president 24 years ago. RBC's Stock sees a "social democrat" who has tightened the fiscal reins before when circumstances demanded it. Schoenfeld frets about new populist promises Lula unveiled in the weeks before his runoff triumph, from retiring small business debt to shortening the official workweek. "The government absolutely can't afford these measures," he says.

The smart money is buying the dip for now, though.

data.description:
To the Editor: Congress has ultimate authority over tariffs, not the president, per Article I of the Constitution ("What a Democratic Congress Would Mean for Wall Street," Cover Story, Oct. 22). Any tariff authority the president has can be rescinded. Whether Congress will do that depends on a lot, but technically it can have the final say over tariffs if it wants to. And I'm sure the Democrats will consider this if a blue wave materializes.

Taylor Barnette On Barrons.com

To the Editor: Raising the capital-gains exclusion from $500,000 to $1 million is long overdue. I don't know what percentage of those who want to sell their homes are holding back because they have gains in excess of $500,000. Regardless, which of our politicians will have the courage to vote in favor of such legislation, knowing that they will be attacked for selling out to the wealthy?

Gary Marton On Barrons.com

'Robust' GDP Growth

To the Editor: "Mixed" results is a very generous characterization ("The Trump Economy in 7 Charts," Oct. 22). The main positive here is stock market performance, but that's an expected result of the massive deficit spending engendered by tax cuts. GDP growth is below the trend of the past 45 years, and hardly "robust." Job creation has been quite weak, per the chart.

Peter Matthews On Barrons.com

It's OK to Be a Renter

To the Editor: Homeownership isn't necessarily slipping away. Americans may simply be unwilling to move, compromise, or consider renting ("Homeownership Helped Make America. It's Slipping Away for Millions," Oct. 18.) Restrictive zoning and glacial permitting processes deserve much of the blame, but so does our collective fixation on living in America's most expensive markets. Nebraska may not offer New York's amenities, and Kansas may lack California's climate, but both provide affordable housing. Government should remove barriers to building, and families should look beyond a handful of high-cost metro areas. Most important, renting is often the financially rational choice, even if decades of real estate industry marketing have convinced Americans otherwise.

Jonathan I. Shenkman West Hempstead, N.Y.

Options ETFs

To the Editor: As a 73-year-old retiree, options ETFs give me exposure to growth plus meaningful income with better returns than traditional fixed income ("Options ETFs Are Booming. Beware the Trade-Offs," Oct. 22). Some use Section 1256 contracts, tax-loss harvesting, and constructive return of capital as a tax classification, and some sell put options, so the upside isn't capped.

data.title: The Smartest People in AI Believe This Is the World's Most Important Chart — WSJ
data.description:
By Ben Cohen

Since the days when artificial intelligence seemed more like fiction than science, one idea has captivated the field's top researchers.

These days, the people leading AI labs believe it could transform their industry, the global economy and perhaps the fate of humanity. OpenAI's chief scientist has called it the only way to remain on the frontier. A co-founder of Anthropic says it "might be the most important technical trend in the world."

And unless you work in AI, you've probably never heard of it.

It's a phenomenon known as "recursive self-improvement," or RSI, which roughly translates to AI building smarter AI. Anthropic refers to it as "closing the loop," a cycle in which each improvement makes the machines better and faster at improving themselves.

AI companies say they are now seeing the early signs of recursive self-improvement, which is speeding up their research — and freaking everyone out. As this technology accelerates its own evolution, the risk is that we struggle to keep pace and keep it under control.

Our best data about this profound shift comes from Anthropic, which recently published a chart showing how much of its AI research and development is being done by AI.

It took a whole village of Claudes to produce the data in this chart. A Claude agent dug through the company's Slack messages and internal documents to identify 15,000 tasks of AI R&D work. A Claude detective investigated exactly how that work was done. Then a Claude judge weighed the evidence and rated the work on a six-level scale, from no AI to fully autonomous AI.

Now take another look at that chart and you'll notice that something extraordinary is happening inside Anthropic.

The most telling bars are the ones in orange for "AI leads," meaning it performs most of the R&D while a human supervises — the fifth of the six levels.

A year ago, AI led none of this work. As recently as March, it only led 1%. By August, Claude was leading 26% of the work on future Claudes. And that number is almost certainly higher today.

Even as the company's researchers delegate to AI, it's worth remembering that 0% of this work is being done entirely by AI. It still hasn't reached the sixth level of automation. But at this rate of progress, AI taking us out of the loop might just be a matter of time, computing power and the decisions of human beings inside the labs.

"We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable," Anthropic recently wrote. "But it could come sooner than most institutions are prepared for."

AI companies have said that models training, testing and fine-tuning the next generation of models is essential to their success. They're also terrified of what that success could mean. Doomers have quit the labs and warned that self-improving AI might kill us all. The field's most prominent researchers have asked for greater oversight and CEOs have called for a slowdown before this rapidly advancing technology reaches full RSI.

"Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has written, "if at all."

But humans have been tantalized by the concept of self-improving AI for the entire history of AI.

When pioneering researchers met at Dartmouth for a summer project in 1956, they were already curious about how machines could improve themselves. As it happens, one of the scientists who proposed that seminal workshop was a Claude — the brilliant mathematician Claude Shannon.

Within a decade, scientists were dreaming about machines that would be smarter than us at everything, including the design of machines.

"Thus," wrote I.J. Good, another brilliant mathematician, "the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control."

Decades later, the men and women bringing that machine to life have never been so worried about their ability to control it. Many of them have been thinking about AI systems autonomously building AI systems since it sounded like sci-fi. They aren't sure what to think now.

"I don't know how to wrap my head around it," Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark recently wrote.

Clark started his career as a tech journalist before he became so obsessed with the story he was covering that he wanted to be part of it. He took a job at a fledgling research lab called OpenAI and eventually left with a small group of colleagues to start Anthropic.

"Ever since, I've been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves," he said in an October speech to the International Monetary Fund. "Well, the moment has arrived."

Only a few months ago, this moment seemed a few years away. It arrived even sooner than Clark expected. After taking parental leave last November, he returned in February to a very different company. While he was changing diapers, Anthropic had changed.

"Weird stuff had started to take place," he wrote in his newsletter.

The company's models were suddenly good enough that engineers had started outsourcing their coding to them and some had stopped writing code altogether.

By May, stuff had gotten so weird, so fast, that he concluded that RSI was likely by the end of 2028. "It's a reluctant view," Clark wrote, "because the implications are so large that I feel dwarfed by them." Then he shortened his timeline again.

He no longer believes 2028 is the most likely year for RSI. He thinks it's 2027.

And you don't need any charts to see what that means: Fiction is on the verge of becoming science.

data.title: The New Bottleneck in America's AI Build-Out: A Shortage of Cheap Money — WSJ
data.description:
By Peter Rudegeair, Robbie Whelan and Jack Pitcher

For years, the companies behind America's artificial-intelligence boom have raised hundreds of billions of dollars with ease. Wall Street eagerly ponied up capital and asked few questions.

Now, the balance of power is shifting.

Lenders and investors are getting choosier about where to place their bets and are demanding tougher terms, signaling a new phase in the AI build-out. Among their concerns: the prospect of delays in big projects as a grassroots political backlash to data centers gains traction, and the threat that AI-related profits from hyperscalers and startups such as Anthropic and OpenAI won't materialize as fast as promised.

Plus, a flood of stock and bond offerings is compounding concerns that investors are getting overexposed to AI.

The new terms of trade are visible in every corner of markets. Bonds issued even by big tech companies such as SpaceX and Meta are trading at steep discounts. AI cloud companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Nscale that borrow big to build and sell capacity have effectively been shut out of the bond market in recent weeks, people familiar with the matter said.

Taken together, it all amounts to a buyer's market for Wall Street. Even powerful players such as Broadcom are having to sweeten the terms offered to banks to secure loans. "The bar is going higher and higher in terms of proving to lenders that this investment will turn into sufficient revenue," said Dan Ivascyn, chief investment officer at Pimco. "The weak links are going to suffer first."

Raising money in equity markets isn't much easier. Nscale's hopes of going public next month have been thwarted, while rival Lambda dialed back the valuation it was seeking in a new fundraising round, people familiar with the matter said.

The stock market is starting to reflect investors' nervousness that the AI payoff might not arrive — at least in the near term. Disappointing earnings reports from technology companies this week prompted a rout in AI-related stocks and bonds, leading Friday to one of the biggest market selloffs since AI-mania began. Google parent Alphabet sustained its largest stock market wipeout ever Thursday, losing roughly $500 billion in market value, after quarterly results showed revenue from its core search business slowing while spending on AI infrastructure continues to surge.

Tremors in the market also shook chip-maker Intel, which saw its share price plummet 29% on Friday after the company reported weakness in its personal computer business. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite dropped 2.9% on Friday, its worst day since June. If the volatility continues, fundraising could grow even harder.

There is still money available for creditworthy companies. SpaceX this week announced it raised the biggest-ever financing for AI chips, a $40 billion package that will allow it to purchase the latest lineup of Nvidia chips.

Its record only lasted a few hours, when chip-design giant Broadcom sealed a $63 billion deal to lease chips to Anthropic. But even that deal showed the strains of the current environment: Broadcom Chief Executive Hock Tan had to personally intervene in negotiations at the last minute to calm banks' nerves.

Even companies that can raise money fret about their suppliers' ability to do so. Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $100 billion in a mid-November offering. In its IPO prospectus unveiled this week, it called out as a risk factor the financing constraints for the electrical-power providers its data centers rely upon.

Meta cited a desire to beat competitors to the punch when it unveiled a plan to raise up to $97.5 billion through a series of new stock offerings. In a securities filing, it pointed to recent and future offerings from the likes of Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI as challenges to the depths of capital markets.

"Everybody is trying to raise money for their build-outs before the liquidity dries up," said Ben Connard, chief investment officer of Carnegie Investment Counsel.

"Ultimately, there might not be enough money to fund this build-out," he said. "Financing could be the ultimate crunch that slows things down."

Customer advances

In the years since ChatGPT launched, AI companies have consumed every source of capital they could find, tapping venture capitalists, stock pickers, bankers and managers of bond and private-credit funds.

Across all types of U.S. corporate debt markets, AI-linked issuance totaled $394 billion in 2025 and $655 billion through mid-October of this year, according to Bank of America. Next year, analysts forecast nearly $1 trillion of fresh AI-linked debt.

Among the most prolific participants in capital markets are so-called neoclouds, companies that own or lease data centers, outfit them with fleets of AI servers and sign contracts to sell computing power to big tech companies, trading firms and AI startups. They are also the most sensitive in the AI sphere to rising interest rates, since their borrowing costs were already elevated before recent turmoil in the market.

Many neoclouds started out as cryptocurrency mining outfits, and most of them have scant histories operating AI infrastructure. Nebius was once the Amsterdam-based company behind Yandex, Russia's top internet company. It divested its main assets following Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and pivoted to providing AI cloud-computing services a little over two years ago, striking contracts with tech companies including Meta and Microsoft.

Since 2024, Nebius has sold some $2.7 billion in stock to Nvidia and other investors and issued billions more in convertible bonds for its AI expansion. But its thirst for capital continues. Over the summer and early fall, Nebius's bankers arranged for company executives to meet with fund managers in advance of a potential high-yield bond offering, people familiar with the matter said. It would have been Nebius's first.

By September, debt markets started to wobble. The Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates for the first time in three years. Challenges over power supply and permitting prompted Oracle to notify the developer of a huge New Mexico data center it previously agreed to lease that it was pushing back the date at which it would pay full rent. That prompted lenders everywhere to re-evaluate construction risk on their projects.

Bonds issued by CoreWeave at a 9.75% rate earlier this year now trade at a yield above 15% in the secondary market, an indication of how much more expensive it has become to borrow over a short period. Bankers cautioned in recent weeks that the high-yield market for neoclouds was essentially shut for new offerings. Yields of 15% or more would be prohibitively expensive for borrowers.

Nebius decided against pursuing a high-yield offering. CEO Arkady Volozh has said his company is having to be increasingly creative to secure the funds needed for its build-out. That includes getting prepayments from its customers.

"From last week, probably some of the capital sources are temporarily closed, like the asset-backed or debt market," Volozh said last week at a conference in Berlin. "But we're working now with customer advances and several other instruments, which will probably provide us enough finance to build this gigawatt at least."

Ophir Nave, chief operating officer of Nebius, said that despite Volozh's comments, the asset-backed financing market remains open, and the company plans to tap it in the future. Whether the company issues high-yield debt will depend on interest rates and the deal terms available to the company, he said.

Equity investors are getting spooked, too. Lambda, which is seeking to raise $4 billion in a final round of pre-IPO fundraising, recently reduced its target valuation from $14.5 billion to $13 billion after investors including tech investment firm Coatue decided not to participate, according to people familiar with the matter.

UK-based neocloud Nscale, which counts former Meta executives Sheryl Sandberg and Nick Clegg as board members, is preparing to go public in the coming months. The company had circled multiple dates on the calendar in November as possible candidates for its IPO, but is now leaning toward December given turbulence in the market, according to people familiar with the company's plans.

Another factor: Nscale is still negotiating with Nvidia and other investors to provide financial backing for a $45 billion data center for Anthropic in West Virginia, according to people familiar with the matter. After the market turned, Nvidia and the other potential backers began demanding more stringent terms, these people said, delaying Nscale's plans to file a revised IPO prospectus. All the uncertainty has convinced Nscale executives that it would be difficult to go public before Anthropic does. Some of the company's bankers have advised Nscale that it's unlikely to attract enough demand in an IPO to achieve the $30 billion to $35 billion valuation they had been targeting, according to people familiar with the matter.

Concentration risks

The largest AI hyperscalers sit on the opposite end of the credit risk spectrum from the neocloud companies, but the sheer scale of their fundraising plans is starting to cause problems.

Meta, Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft carry top credit ratings and have significant room to pile debt on their balance sheets. But after many of them flooded the high-grade debt market with new bond sales this year — and signaled they plan to keep doing so for the foreseeable future — the investment firms, insurance companies and pension funds that lend to them are feeling increasingly tapped out, and concerned about their concentration in one sector.

"There's just the practical question of, how full can investors get on one name, or one theme?" said Pimco's Ivascyn.
